title: Is Low Hemoglobin a Sign of Cancer? What a Low Result Usually Means
summary: Is low hemoglobin a sign of cancer? Which cancers cause anemia, the far more common causes, how MCV and ferritin narrow it down, and who needs a GI evaluation.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


Low hemoglobin is usually not a sign of cancer. Low hemoglobin means anemia, and MedlinePlus \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/anemia.html) \] names not having enough iron as its most common cause. Iron deficiency most often comes from low intake, heavy periods, pregnancy or slow blood loss \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32809711/) \]. Cancer can lower hemoglobin, mainly through slow bleeding from the digestive tract or by crowding the bone marrow, but it is one possible cause among many. The rest of your complete blood count (CBC), especially red cell size (MCV), together with ferritin, shows which kind of anemia you have and whether a cancer evaluation makes sense.


For the general symptoms of a low result, see[low hemoglobin symptoms and what the result means](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-hemoglobin) . For reference ranges, see the[hemoglobin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/hemoglobin) ,[MCV](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/mcv) and[ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/ferritin) overviews. This page answers one question: could a low hemoglobin mean cancer, and how do you find out?


## The short answer


- **Iron deficiency is the usual cause.** Anemia has three main causes: blood loss, too little red blood cell production, and red cells being destroyed too fast. Not having enough iron is the most common \[[1](https://medlineplus.gov/anemia.html) \].
- **Cancer is a less common cause, but a real one.** The cancers most linked with low hemoglobin are digestive tract cancers that bleed slowly, and bone marrow cancers such as leukemia, lymphoma and multiple myeloma \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003133.htm) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000560.htm) \]. Kidney cancer and the long-term inflammation of cancer can lower it too.
- **Who you are matters.** In premenopausal women, iron deficiency anemia usually reflects menstrual loss or pregnancy. In men and postmenopausal women, it is often due to slow blood loss from the digestive tract, and British guidelines report that about a third have an underlying abnormality, most commonly in the gut \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \].
- **The pattern points the way.** Small red cells with low ferritin point to iron deficiency. Large red cells point to B12 or folate problems. Normal-sized cells, or low white cells or platelets as well, point toward chronic disease or the bone marrow.


## Which cancers cause low hemoglobin, and how


Cancer lowers hemoglobin in a few distinct ways. Each one leaves a different pattern on blood tests.


### Slow bleeding from the digestive tract


Cancers of the colon, stomach and small intestine can bleed \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003133.htm) \]. Slow, unseen bleeding drains the body’s iron, which eventually causes iron deficiency anemia with small red cells and a low ferritin. The British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) notes that iron deficiency anemia may be the first sign of colon or esophageal and stomach cancer, often without other symptoms \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \]. The National Cancer Institute lists blood in the stool, a change in bowel habits, weight loss for no known reason and fatigue among the signs of colon cancer \[[6](https://www.cancer.gov/types/colorectal/patient/colon-treatment-pdq) \].


This is the route that matters most for someone with no known cancer, and it is why unexplained iron deficiency is taken seriously in some groups (see “Who needs a GI evaluation” below).


### Cancers in the bone marrow


Red blood cells are made in the bone marrow. MedlinePlus lists lymphoma, leukemia, myelodysplasia and multiple myeloma among the bone marrow problems that cause anemia \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000560.htm) \]. In acute myeloid leukemia, leukemia cells crowd out healthy red cells, white cells and platelets, which can cause anemia, infections and easy bleeding \[[7](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/adult-aml-treatment-pdq) \]. In multiple myeloma, fewer red cells, white cells and platelets are made as myeloma cells increase, and myeloma is sometimes found on a blood or urine test done for another reason \[[8](https://www.cancer.gov/types/myeloma/patient/myeloma-treatment-pdq) \].


Marrow problems usually show as a low reticulocyte count, because the marrow is not producing enough new red cells \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31082147/) \]. They can also lower white cells or platelets on the same CBC, which iron deficiency does not explain.


### Kidney cancer and kidney disease


The kidneys make erythropoietin (EPO), the hormone that tells the marrow to make red cells. When kidney function falls, the EPO response is blunted and anemia follows \[[10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29763170/) \]. The National Cancer Institute lists anemia among the signs of kidney cancer, alongside blood in the urine, a lump in the abdomen, side pain that does not go away, and weight loss for no known reason \[[11](https://www.cancer.gov/types/kidney/patient/kidney-treatment-pdq) \].


### Inflammation from cancer and other chronic disease


Cancer, chronic kidney disease, infection and autoimmune disease can all lead the body to make fewer red blood cells \[[12](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/causes) \]. In this anemia of chronic disease, also called anemia of inflammation, iron stores are adequate but locked away and unavailable for making red cells \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32809711/) \]. Anemia with normal-sized red cells most commonly results from chronic infections and systemic diseases \[[13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33351438/) \]. The same kind of anemia occurs with rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and other chronic inflammatory conditions, so it does not point to cancer on its own \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \].


### Cancer treatment


For people already being treated, chemotherapy and radiation therapy are common causes of anemia \[[14](https://www.cancer.gov/about-cancer/treatment/side-effects/anemia) \]. That is a different situation from a low result on routine blood work, and the oncology team manages it.


## Low hemoglobin without cancer: the common causes


Most people with low hemoglobin do not have cancer. MedlinePlus and the NHLBI list these causes \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000560.htm) \]\[[12](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/causes) \]:


- **Iron deficiency** from low intake, heavy menstrual periods, pregnancy, blood donation, or slow bleeding from a stomach ulcer or inflamed bowel.
- **Poor iron absorption** , for example from celiac disease or stomach surgery. The BSG reports celiac disease in 3% to 5% of people investigated for unexplained iron deficiency anemia \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \].
- **Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency** , which makes large red cells. The[B12 and cancer article](https://mitohealth.com/blog/can-b12-deficiency-be-a-sign-of-cancer) covers that branch.
- **Chronic conditions** such as chronic kidney disease, rheumatoid arthritis and ulcerative colitis.
- **Inherited conditions** such as thalassemia trait and sickle cell disease.
- **Hemolysis** , when red cells are destroyed early, for example by an immune reaction, an infection or a medicine \[[15](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000571.htm) \].
- **Certain medicines.**


Even among people who are investigated because guidelines say they should be, cancer is the minority finding. In men and postmenopausal women investigated for iron deficiency anemia, the BSG reports that cancer is found in 8% to 10%, and that most investigations find no other significant abnormality either \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \]. Mild anemia may cause no symptoms at all \[[16](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/anemia/symptoms) \], so it may first show up on a routine blood count.


## What your CBC pattern suggests


A low hemoglobin on its own does not tell you the cause. The rest of the CBC and a few related tests narrow it down. Anemia is classified by MCV, the average size of the red cells \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31082147/) \]:


Pattern What it usually suggests


Low MCV (small cells) with low ferritin Iron deficiency. The next question is where the iron went, which is where blood loss, including from the gut, comes in \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \]


Low MCV with normal ferritin and iron studies Thalassemia trait is one explanation, and the BSG recommends hemoglobin electrophoresis here to avoid unneeded GI tests \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \]. Anemia of chronic disease and, less often, lead exposure are others \[[2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32809711/) \]


High MCV (large cells) Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency is the classic cause, though there are others \[[17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29083571/) \]


Normal MCV Anemia of chronic disease, kidney disease, early iron deficiency, aplastic anemia, or marrow infiltration \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31082147/) \]


Low white cells or platelets as well Points to a problem in the bone marrow itself, which needs prompt clinical review \[[7](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/adult-aml-treatment-pdq) \]\[[18](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000554.htm) \]


Low[reticulocyte count](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/reticulocyte-count) The marrow is not making enough new red cells, as in nutrient deficiency, chronic disease or marrow disorders. A high count suggests bleeding or red cell destruction \[[9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31082147/) \]


Two details change how ferritin is read:


- **Ferritin is the most useful single test for iron deficiency.** The BSG calls it the single most useful marker \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \]. In people with anemia, the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) recommends a ferritin cutoff of 45 ng/mL rather than 15 ng/mL to diagnose iron deficiency \[[19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32810434/) \].
- **Inflammation can hide iron deficiency.** Ferritin rises with inflammation, so it can look normal even when iron is low. Transferrin saturation helps when that is suspected \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \]. This is also why anemia of chronic disease can be mistaken for iron deficiency, and the reverse.


For what a low result on each marker can mean, see[low MCV](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-mcv) and[low ferritin](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-ferritin) .


## Who needs a GI evaluation


Unexplained iron deficiency anemia in men and in women after menopause is the situation where a cancer search is routine. Both major gastroenterology guidelines say so:


- **The AGA (2020)** recommends bidirectional endoscopy, meaning an upper endoscopy and a colonoscopy, over no endoscopy for men and postmenopausal women with iron deficiency anemia and no symptoms. For premenopausal women without symptoms, it suggests the same evaluation over iron treatment alone, as a conditional recommendation. It also suggests blood tests for celiac disease where celiac disease is plausible \[[20](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/) \].
- **The BSG (2021)** recommends that men and postmenopausal women with newly diagnosed iron deficiency anemia generally have a gastroscopy and colonoscopy first, along with a urine test and celiac screening. In premenopausal women, it says GI investigation is generally not needed when nothing else points to it, because menstrual loss or recent pregnancy is the likely cause. It lowers that threshold for women over 50, people with GI symptoms, and people with a family history of GI disease \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \].


The two guidelines differ for premenopausal women, so that decision is worth discussing directly with a clinician.


The BSG notes that investigation should be considered at any level of anemia when iron deficiency is confirmed, not only when hemoglobin is very low \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \]. This evaluation is different from routine colorectal cancer screening. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force screening recommendation applies to adults 45 and older without symptoms who are at average risk \[[21](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/colorectal-cancer-screening) \]. Unexplained iron deficiency anemia is a reason for a diagnostic workup, which a clinician orders.


## Symptoms that need same-day care


MedlinePlus advises calling 911 or going to the emergency room for black, tarry stools, a lot of blood in the stool, vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, feeling lightheaded or dizzy from bleeding, chest pain or trouble breathing, or severe abdominal pain with bleeding \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003133.htm) \]. These need care whatever your hemoglobin number is.


Contact a clinician promptly, rather than waiting on more tests, if a low hemoglobin comes with weight loss for no known reason, a change in bowel habits, blood in the urine, frequent infections, easy bruising or bleeding, or bone pain. These are among the signs the National Cancer Institute lists for colon cancer, kidney cancer, leukemia and myeloma \[[6](https://www.cancer.gov/types/colorectal/patient/colon-treatment-pdq) \]\[[7](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/adult-aml-treatment-pdq) \]\[[8](https://www.cancer.gov/types/myeloma/patient/myeloma-treatment-pdq) \]\[[11](https://www.cancer.gov/types/kidney/patient/kidney-treatment-pdq) \].


## Tests that come next


MedlinePlus lists the CBC, the reticulocyte count, and blood levels of iron, vitamin B12 and folate among the blood tests for anemia \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000560.htm) \]. These are the tests that separate the patterns above.

Some tests are for a clinician to order once the blood work points somewhere: celiac antibodies, a urine test for blood, hemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected thalassemia, upper endoscopy and colonoscopy for unexplained iron deficiency, and bone marrow evaluation when the counts suggest a marrow problem \[[5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34497146/) \]\[[7](https://www.cancer.gov/types/leukemia/patient/adult-aml-treatment-pdq) \]. Taking iron without knowing the cause can delay finding a source of bleeding, so confirm the cause first.


## What to ask a clinician


- Is my low hemoglobin confirmed on a repeat CBC, and what are my MCV, white cell count and platelets?
- Is my ferritin low, and could inflammation be making a normal ferritin misleading?
- If I have iron deficiency, where is the iron going? Do I need an upper endoscopy and colonoscopy, given my age, sex and symptoms?
- Should I be checked for celiac disease or blood in the urine?
- If my red cells are large, or my reticulocyte count is low, which tests come next?
- If other cell lines are low too, should I see a hematologist?

## Frequently asked questions


### Does low hemoglobin mean you have cancer?


No. Low hemoglobin means anemia, and anemia has many causes. Not having enough iron is the most common one. Cancer is one possible cause, so the useful step is to find out why hemoglobin is low, starting with the rest of the blood count and ferritin.


### Can you have low hemoglobin without cancer?


Yes, and most people with low hemoglobin do. Iron deficiency from diet, heavy periods, pregnancy or a stomach ulcer, vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, chronic kidney disease, inflammatory conditions, inherited conditions such as thalassemia trait, and some medicines can all lower it.


### What cancer starts with anemia?


Cancers of the colon and stomach can first show up as iron deficiency anemia from slow, unnoticed bleeding, often without other symptoms. Blood cancers such as leukemia and multiple myeloma can lower hemoglobin by crowding out normal blood cell production in the bone marrow, and the National Cancer Institute lists anemia among the signs of kidney cancer.


### Is microcytic anemia a sign of cancer?


Microcytic anemia, where red cells are smaller than normal, most often means iron deficiency. In men and postmenopausal women, unexplained iron deficiency anemia is a reason for a clinician to check the digestive tract for bleeding, which can include cancer. Thalassemia trait and anemia of chronic disease can also cause small red cells, so iron studies come first.


### Does anemia mean cancer has spread?


Not by itself. In people who already have cancer, anemia can come from chemotherapy or radiation, from bleeding, or from a cancer that involves the bone marrow. The care team works out which cause applies. Anemia alone does not show the stage.


### What stage of colon cancer causes anemia?


There is no single stage. A colon cancer can bleed slowly enough to cause iron deficiency without other symptoms, and iron deficiency anemia can be the first sign. Stage is set by how far the cancer has grown and spread, which is found with colonoscopy, imaging and pathology, not with a hemoglobin result.


### Is aplastic anemia cancer?


No. Aplastic anemia is a bone marrow failure condition in which the marrow does not make enough red cells, white cells and platelets. Causes include some medicines and chemicals, radiation or chemotherapy, autoimmune disorders and viruses, and sometimes no cause is found. It is serious and is treated by blood specialists.


### Is hemolytic anemia cancer?


No. In hemolytic anemia, red blood cells are destroyed earlier than normal, for example by the immune system, an infection, a medicine, or an inherited red cell defect. It usually shows a high reticulocyte count, because the bone marrow is working hard to replace the lost cells.
